title: November Examination: Paper 3 (Writing)
instructions: This question paper consists of TWO sections: SECTION A: Essay (QUESTION 1, 50 marks) and SECTION B: Transactional texts (QUESTION 2, 25 marks, and QUESTION 3, 25 marks).
Answer ONE topic from QUESTION 1, ONE option from QUESTION 2 and ONE option from QUESTION 3. You will write THREE texts in total.
Write all your answers in English.

You must plan each answer (for example with a mind map, flow diagram or list of key points). Your planning must appear BEFORE each text and must be neatly crossed out once you have written the final version.
Write down the letter and the title or text type of each topic you choose exactly as it appears in this question paper.
Keep to the required length: SECTION A, 400 to 450 words; SECTION B, 180 to 200 words for each text (count only the body of the text).
Start each question on a NEW page.
Pay special attention to spelling, punctuation, grammar and sentence construction. Edit and proofread your work before you hand it in.
Suggested time: SECTION A, about 80 minutes; SECTION B, about 35 minutes for each question.
Using this app: write your answers on paper or in a word processor, then open the memo for each question and use the rubric to award your own marks (or ask a teacher to mark your work).

questions.prompt:
Write an essay of between 400 and 450 words on ONE of the following topics. Write down the letter and the title of the topic you have chosen. For topics F, G and H, also give your essay a suitable title of your own.

**A.** The parcel that arrived on the wrong doorstep
[Write a narrative essay.]

**B.** Waiting for the storm: a summer afternoon on the Highveld
[Write a descriptive essay.]

**C.** Matric results should never be published in newspapers or online.
[Write an argumentative essay in which you argue FOR or AGAINST this statement.]

**D.** Artificial intelligence is a friend, not a foe, to South African learners.
[Write a discursive essay in which you discuss both sides of this statement.]

**E.** What the people who raised me taught me without saying a word
[Write a reflective essay.]

**F.** "We know what we are, but know not what we may be." (Ophelia, in William Shakespeare's *Hamlet*, Act 4, Scene 5)
[Write an essay of any type in response to this quotation.]

**G.** Picture G (above)
[Interpret the picture in any way you choose and write an essay of any type. Your essay must clearly relate to the picture.]

**H.** Picture H (above)
[Interpret the picture in any way you choose and write an essay of any type. Your essay must clearly relate to the picture.]

Plan your essay before you start writing, and edit and proofread it when you have finished.
questions.memo:
**MARKING GUIDELINES: QUESTION 1 (ESSAY)**
Mark the essay with the rubric below. Read the whole essay first, decide on a level for each of the three criteria, and then award a mark within that level. Credit original, well-crafted responses that interpret a topic differently from the guidance, as long as the link to the topic is clear and purposeful.

- **Essay type:** for topics A to E the essay type is specified. A response written in a different type (e.g. a story for topic C, or a one-sided essay for topic D) has not met the requirements of the topic, and its Content and planning mark should not go beyond the Moderate level.
- **Length:** an essay far shorter than 400 words usually lacks the development needed for the higher Content and Structure levels; an essay far longer than 450 words shows weak planning and editing. Estimate the length; do not count every word.
- **Planning:** planning must be shown before the essay.

**GUIDANCE ON THE TOPICS**

**A. The parcel that arrived on the wrong doorstep (narrative)**
- A clear plot: an opening that establishes character and setting, a complication caused by the parcel, rising tension, a climax and a resolution.
- The parcel should drive the conflict, e.g. curiosity about its contents, the temptation to keep it, a mystery, a moral choice about returning it, or an unexpected connection with the person for whom it was meant.
- The title may also be read figuratively (news, a secret or a responsibility that reached the wrong person).
- Credit believable characters, purposeful and correctly punctuated dialogue, a consistent narrative voice and tense, and a satisfying or thought-provoking ending.
- A bare list of events, or an ending that cancels the story ("and then I woke up"), cannot reach the higher levels.

**B. Waiting for the storm: a summer afternoon on the Highveld (descriptive)**
- A vivid word picture of the build-up to an afternoon thunderstorm: oppressive heat, towering clouds, the changing light, gusts of dust, the smell of rain on dry earth, distant thunder, the first heavy drops.
- People, animals and places reacting to the coming storm, e.g. washing pulled off the line, hadedas calling, hawkers covering their stalls, taxis hooting.
- Appeal to all five senses; precise, fresh vocabulary; figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification, onomatopoeia) used with purpose rather than piled up.
- A controlling mood (tension, expectation, relief) and a clear organising principle, e.g. chronological, or moving from a wide view to close-up detail.
- There should be little plot. An essay that is mainly a story is narrative, not descriptive.

**C. Matric results should never be published in newspapers or online (argumentative)**
- ONE clear stand, stated in the introduction and maintained throughout.
- FOR the statement, possible arguments: results are personal information and learners have a right to privacy (learners may refer to the Protection of Personal Information Act, POPIA); public results add to stress and shame and may harm mental health; learners can be bullied or mocked; results are available privately through schools and official channels.
- AGAINST the statement, possible arguments: publication is a long tradition that lets communities celebrate success together; it makes schools accountable to the public; it motivates younger learners; results can be published by examination number rather than by name, which protects privacy.
- Each paragraph develops one argument with reasons and examples; the strongest essays anticipate and rebut the opposing view.
- Persuasive techniques (rhetorical questions, emotive but controlled language, direct address, repetition) and a conclusion that restates the stand forcefully.

**D. Artificial intelligence is a friend, not a foe, to South African learners (discursive)**
- A balanced discussion of BOTH sides. The introduction presents the issue without taking a firm side.
- Possible arguments that AI is a friend: personalised explanations and practice at any time of day; help for learners in schools with few resources or large classes; translation between languages; support for learners with disabilities; faster research.
- Possible arguments that AI is a foe: cheating and plagiarism; over-reliance that weakens thinking and writing skills; confident but incorrect answers; privacy concerns about personal data; unequal access because of the cost of data and devices.
- A measured, mostly impersonal tone; linking words that weigh ideas (however, on the other hand, nevertheless).
- The conclusion may offer a reasoned, balanced judgement. An essay that argues only one side is argumentative, not discursive.

**E. What the people who raised me taught me without saying a word (reflective)**
- The "people who raised me" may be parents, grandparents, guardians, older siblings, an aunt or uncle, or a community.
- The focus is on lessons taught by example, e.g. a grandmother who rose before dawn to work, a father who apologised when he was wrong, a guardian who shared what little they had.
- Specific moments and memories are used as a springboard for thought, not simply retold: the writer examines what these moments mean and how they have shaped their values, habits and identity.
- Honest, sincere first-person voice; the essay may acknowledge mixed or painful lessons. The conclusion shows insight or growth.
- An essay that is only a list of lessons, or only a story, cannot reach the higher levels.

**F. "We know what we are, but know not what we may be." (any type)**
- Possible interpretations: no one knows their own potential; people can change and grow beyond their circumstances; identity is not fixed; the future is uncertain and may hold great good or great harm; the uncertainty after matric.
- Any essay type is acceptable, e.g. a narrative of an unexpected transformation, a reflective essay about who the writer may become, an argumentative essay that a person's background should not limit their future.
- The quotation must be the springboard of the essay and the link must be clear. The learner does not need to know the context of the line in the play. An essay that only retells or analyses *Hamlet* has misread the task.

**G. Picture G: the fork in the road with blank signs (any type)**
- Possible interpretations: an important choice with no guidance (after matric, careers, friendships, peer pressure); the freedom, and the fear, of choosing one's own path; decisions made without knowing the outcome; having to create one's own direction because no one else can.
- The blank signs are a key detail; essays that use them meaningfully deserve credit.
- Credit original interpretations that go beyond the predictable "two roads" cliché. The essay must have a title, and the connection to the picture must be clear, even if it is not literal.

**H. Picture H: the staircase to an open door (any type)**
- Possible interpretations: reaching a goal one step at a time; education as a way up; opportunity and a new beginning; the unknown future; hope (the light); ambition; the idea that a destination may be different from what one expects (the door stands alone and nothing beyond it is visible).
- Any essay type is acceptable. The essay must have a title, and the connection to the picture must be clear, even if it is not literal.

**ESSAY RUBRIC (50 marks)**

**Content and planning (30 marks)**
- **25 to 30, Exceptional:** content shows impressive insight and originality and is fully relevant to the topic; ideas are mature and thought-provoking; planning has produced a coherent essay in which every paragraph contributes; all requirements of the essay type are met.
- **19 to 24, Skilful:** content is interesting, relevant and shows some originality; ideas are well developed; planning is evident and the essay is coherent; the features of the essay type are clearly present.
- **13 to 18, Moderate:** content is ordinary but relevant; some ideas are repetitive or underdeveloped; the sequence is reasonable but predictable; the essay type is recognisable.
- **7 to 12, Elementary:** content is dull or only loosely relevant; ideas are thin, repetitive or muddled; little evidence of planning; the essay type is unclear.
- **0 to 6, Inadequate:** content is irrelevant or confused; no evidence of planning; the topic and essay type are not addressed.

**Language, style and editing (15 marks)**
- **13 to 15, Exceptional:** tone, register, style and vocabulary are highly appropriate and controlled; sentence structure is varied and effective; figurative language is purposeful; grammar, spelling and punctuation are virtually error-free.
- **10 to 12, Skilful:** language is fluent and appropriate; vocabulary is varied; very few errors.
- **7 to 9, Moderate:** language is adequate; register is mostly appropriate; some errors, but meaning is clear.
- **4 to 6, Elementary:** vocabulary is basic and limited; register is often inappropriate; frequent errors that sometimes obscure meaning.
- **0 to 3, Inadequate:** so many errors that meaning is largely lost.

**Structure (5 marks)**
- **5, Exceptional:** excellent paragraphing with clear topic sentences; logical development; smooth transitions; correct length.
- **4, Skilful:** well-organised paragraphs and a logical sequence; correct length.
- **3, Moderate:** paragraphing mostly sound; sequence sometimes weak; length roughly correct.
- **2, Elementary:** poor paragraphing; ideas loosely connected; noticeably too short or too long.
- **0 to 1, Inadequate:** no paragraphing or coherence; far too short.

**CALCULATING THE MARK**
Content and planning ✓ (30) + Language, style and editing ✓ (15) + Structure ✓ (5) = 50 marks

context.title: Advertisement for Option B (written for this paper; the organisation is fictitious)
context.text:
**UMOYA COASTAL CONSERVATION TRUST**
**Youth Ranger Assistants wanted for the summer holidays**

Do you love the ocean? Can you explain things clearly to people of all ages? Join our turtle-protection and beach-education programme on the KwaZulu-Natal north coast from 1 December to 31 January.

**Your duties will include:**
- guiding visitors along beach trails and explaining how to protect nesting turtles
- recording the litter collected during daily beach clean-ups
- helping trained rangers to monitor turtle nests at night
- presenting short talks to holiday groups and children

**Requirements:**
- You must be in Grade 12 this year or have completed Grade 12.
- You must speak English and at least one other South African language well.
- You must be fit enough to walk long distances on sand.
- First-aid training and the ability to swim are an advantage.

**We offer:** a monthly stipend of R4 500, shared accommodation, meals and a certificate of completion.

Send a letter of application, together with a short CV and the names of two referees, to: Ms N. Dlamini, Programme Coordinator, Umoya Coastal Conservation Trust, PO Box 1187, Mtunzini.

**Closing date: 30 November**

questions.prompt:
Write ONE of the following texts. The body of your text must be between 180 and 200 words. Write down the letter and the type of text you have chosen (e.g. B. Formal letter of application). Use the correct format, register and tone for your audience and purpose.

**A. Letter to the press**
Your local municipality has announced that, to save money, the community library in your town will open only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from next year, and will no longer open on Saturdays. Write a letter to the editor of your local newspaper in which you express your views on this decision.

**B. Formal letter of application**
Read the advertisement above. Write a letter in which you apply for a position as a Youth Ranger Assistant.

**C. Friendly letter**
Three months ago your best friend and their family moved from Polokwane to Auckland, New Zealand. In a recent voice note your friend admitted to feeling very homesick and lonely. Write a letter to your friend in which you share news from home and encourage them.

**D. Formal speech**
You have been chosen to deliver the valedictory (farewell) speech on behalf of the Grade 12 class at your school's valedictory ceremony. Parents, teachers and members of the school governing body will attend. Write the speech you will deliver.
questions.memo:
**MARKING GUIDELINES: QUESTION 2**
Mark the text with the transactional rubric below. Format is assessed under Content, planning and format. Count only the body of the text for length: addresses, dates, salutations and endings are not counted.

**A. Letter to the press**
Format:
- Sender's address in the top right-hand corner, followed by the date
- Recipient: The Editor, followed by the name and address of the newspaper (left margin)
- Salutation: Sir/Madam or Dear Editor
- Subject line, e.g. RE: SHORTER LIBRARY HOURS WILL HURT OUR COMMUNITY
- Ending: Yours faithfully, signature and full name (the town or suburb may be added below the name)
Content:
- States the issue and the writer's position clearly in the first paragraph.
- Supports the view with reasons, e.g. many learners have no quiet place to study at home; job seekers rely on the library's free computers and internet; Saturday is the only day on which many working people and schoolchildren can visit; the library is a safe space for children; reading builds literacy in the community.
- Acknowledges the municipality's budget problem and suggests realistic alternatives, e.g. trained volunteers, sponsorship by local businesses, shorter weekday hours instead of closing on Saturdays, a community fundraising drive.
- Ends with a clear call to action, e.g. asking the municipality to reconsider or inviting residents to attend a public meeting.
Register: formal, polite but firm; persuasive without being insulting.

**B. Formal letter of application**
Format:
- Sender's address in the top right-hand corner, followed by the date
- Recipient's title and address: Ms N. Dlamini, Programme Coordinator, Umoya Coastal Conservation Trust, PO Box 1187, Mtunzini
- Salutation: Dear Ms Dlamini or Dear Sir/Madam
- Subject line: APPLICATION FOR THE POSITION OF YOUTH RANGER ASSISTANT
- Ending: Yours faithfully (Yours sincerely is also acceptable when the person is addressed by name), signature and full name
Content:
- Names the position and says where the advertisement was seen.
- Explains why the writer wants the position, e.g. a love of marine life, an interest in conservation, or a future career in environmental science or tourism.
- Shows with evidence that the writer meets EACH requirement: Grade 12 status; the languages spoken (e.g. English and isiZulu); fitness (sport, hiking); first-aid training or swimming ability if any; experience of speaking to groups (e.g. guiding at school open days, debating, the Eco-Club).
- Confirms availability for the whole period, 1 December to 31 January.
- Mentions the enclosed CV and referees, gives contact details and asks for an interview.
Register: formal, confident and courteous; no boasting, no slang, and no copying of the advertisement word for word.

**C. Friendly letter**
Format:
- Sender's address and the date in the top right-hand corner (no recipient's address)
- Informal salutation, e.g. Dear Naledi,
- Informal ending, e.g. Missing you lots, or Your friend always, followed by the writer's first name
Content:
- Opens warmly and responds with empathy to the voice note, reassuring the friend that homesickness is normal.
- Shares specific, lively news from home: school and the matric year, mutual friends, family, events in Polokwane.
- Offers encouragement and practical suggestions, e.g. joining a club, sports team or youth group; regular video calls; exploring the new city; giving it time.
- Recalls a shared memory and looks forward to future contact or a visit.
Register: warm, friendly and conversational; contractions and gentle humour are suitable, but the language must still be correct (no SMS language).

**D. Formal speech**
Format and features (a speech has no addresses or date):
- Opens by greeting the audience appropriately, e.g. "Principal, members of the School Governing Body, teachers, parents and fellow matriculants, good evening."
- An introduction that captures attention (an anecdote, a question or a striking statement) and makes the purpose of the speech clear.
- A conclusion that leaves the audience with a memorable message, followed by thanks, e.g. "Thank you."
Content:
- Reflects on the class's journey from Grade 8 to Grade 12: shared memories, achievements and challenges overcome.
- Thanks teachers, parents and support staff sincerely and specifically.
- Speaks on behalf of the whole class (we, us, our) and looks ahead to the future with hope and advice.
- Uses devices suited to listeners: direct address, rhetorical questions, repetition, groups of three, appropriate humour.
Register: formal yet warm and sincere; suitable for a mixed audience of adults and learners; no private jokes that exclude the audience.

**TRANSACTIONAL TEXT RUBRIC (25 marks)**

**Content, planning and format (15 marks)**
- **13 to 15, Exceptional:** insightful, original and fully relevant response; purpose, audience and context fully understood; format conventions applied correctly; clearly well planned.
- **10 to 12, Skilful:** relevant, well-developed content; good awareness of purpose and audience; format correct with minor lapses.
- **7 to 9, Moderate:** adequate, relevant content; some awareness of audience; format mostly correct, with some errors or omissions.
- **4 to 6, Elementary:** thin or partly irrelevant content; little awareness of audience; format poorly applied.
- **0 to 3, Inadequate:** irrelevant or confused content; no awareness of format.

**Language, style and editing (10 marks)**
- **9 to 10, Exceptional:** register, tone and style perfectly suited to the purpose and audience; precise vocabulary; virtually error-free.
- **7 to 8, Skilful:** appropriate register; fluent; few errors.
- **5 to 6, Moderate:** register mostly appropriate; adequate language; some errors.
- **3 to 4, Elementary:** register often inappropriate; frequent errors.
- **0 to 2, Inadequate:** so many errors that meaning is largely lost.

**CALCULATING THE MARK**
Content, planning and format ✓ (15) + Language, style and editing ✓ (10) = 25 marks

context.title: Notes for Option B: the wetland clean-up (written for this paper; all people and organisations are fictitious)
context.text:
- **What:** a clean-up of the wetland and stream behind the school, organised by the school's Eco-Club
- **When:** Saturday, 24 October, from 07:30 to 13:00
- **Who:** 86 volunteers (learners, parents, teachers and members of two church youth groups), supported by the ward councillor's office and GreenLoop Recycling, a local company that supplied gloves and bags
- **Results:** 112 bags of litter collected, about 40% of it plastic bottles and packets (sent for recycling); 14 old tyres, a shopping trolley and a fridge door were also pulled out of the reeds
- **Highlight:** by the afternoon a grey heron was seen fishing in the cleared stretch of water
- **Ayanda Mokoena, Eco-Club chairperson (Grade 11):** "We were shocked by how much plastic was hidden in the reeds. The stream can breathe again."
- **Johan Pretorius, resident (68):** "I have lived here for forty years and I haven't seen the water this clear since I was a young man."
- **Next steps:** monthly clean-ups; the club has asked the municipality for more bins near the taxi rank; the next clean-up is on Saturday, 28 November

questions.prompt:
Write ONE of the following texts. The body of your text must be between 180 and 200 words. Write down the letter and the type of text you have chosen. Use the correct format, register and tone for your audience and purpose.

**A. Review**
Your school magazine has an entertainment page. Write a review of a film, television series, book, music album or video game that you have recently watched, read, listened to or played.

**B. Newspaper article**
Use the notes for Option B above to write an article for your local community newspaper about the wetland clean-up organised by your school's Eco-Club.

**C. Dialogue**
You would like to take a gap year after matric to work and save money before you study further. Your parent or guardian wants you to go straight to university or college next year. Write the dialogue between you and your parent or guardian.

**D. Minutes of a meeting**
You are the secretary of your school's Grade 12 Farewell Committee. Use the rough notes for Option D above to write the minutes of the committee's most recent meeting.
questions.memo:
**MARKING GUIDELINES: QUESTION 3**
Mark the text with the transactional rubric below. Format is assessed under Content, planning and format. Count only the body of the text for length.

**A. Review**
Format and features:
- An eye-catching heading for the review
- Key details of the work: title, genre, director, author, artist or developer, platform or publisher, and the age restriction where relevant
- The reviewer's name (by-line)
- A rating, e.g. 4/5 stars or 7/10
Content:
- A brief overview of the plot or content that does NOT give away the ending.
- Evaluation supported by specific examples, e.g. acting and characterisation, storyline and pacing, visuals, soundtrack, writing style, gameplay.
- A balanced judgement that mentions strengths and weaknesses.
- A clear recommendation that names the audience most likely to enjoy the work.
Register: lively, semi-formal and evaluative (e.g. gripping, predictable, understated); mainly in the present tense; aimed at fellow learners. A review that only retells the story cannot reach the higher levels.

**B. Newspaper article**
Format:
- Headline: short and attention-grabbing, e.g. Learners Give Wetland a New Lease on Life
- By-line: By [name]
- Optional: the place and date, sub-headings, a photo caption
Content:
- The lead (first) paragraph answers who, what, when, where and why: the school's Eco-Club cleaned up the wetland and stream behind the school on Saturday, 24 October.
- The following paragraphs give the details in order of importance and use the facts from the notes accurately: 86 volunteers; support from the ward councillor's office and GreenLoop Recycling; 112 bags of litter, about 40% of it plastic; 14 tyres, a shopping trolley and a fridge door; the grey heron.
- At least one direct quotation from the notes, correctly punctuated and attributed, e.g. Ayanda Mokoena, the Eco-Club's chairperson, said: "We were shocked by how much plastic was hidden in the reeds."
- Ends with the next steps: monthly clean-ups, the request for more bins near the taxi rank, and the next clean-up on Saturday, 28 November.
Register: objective and factual; third person; past tense for the event; short paragraphs; no personal opinions using "I". Facts that contradict the notes count against the content mark.

**C. Dialogue**
Format:
- A brief description of the setting before the dialogue begins, e.g. (The kitchen after supper. Mama is drying the dishes.)
- Speakers' names on the left, followed by a colon; a new line for each speaker
- No quotation marks
- Stage directions in brackets, in the present tense, used sparingly to show tone or action, e.g. (sighs)
Content:
- Both points of view are developed convincingly. The learner might argue: gaining work experience, saving money for fees, becoming more mature, choosing a career with more certainty, avoiding an expensive wrong choice of course. The parent might argue: the risk of losing momentum and never returning to study, missing application and bursary or NSFAS deadlines, the cost of living, time wasted.
- The conversation develops logically and reaches a resolution or compromise, e.g. a gap year with a written plan, while applications are still submitted for the following year.
- Each speaker has a distinct, believable voice, and the exchange stays respectful.
Register: natural spoken English that suits the relationship; informal but not full of slang; the language must still be correct.

**D. Minutes of a meeting**
Format:
- Heading, e.g. Minutes of the meeting of the Grade 12 Farewell Committee of [name of school], held on Thursday, 10 September 2026 at 14:00 in Room 12
- Present and Apologies
- Numbered items, e.g. 1. Welcome and opening; 2. Minutes of the previous meeting; 3. Matters arising; 4. Treasurer's report; 5. New business; 6. General; 7. Date of next meeting; 8. Closure
- Signature lines for the chairperson and the secretary, with dates
Content (must match the notes accurately):
- The chairperson, Lerato Khumalo, welcomed members and opened the meeting at 14:05; an apology was received from Kagiso Molefe.
- The minutes of the meeting of 27 August were accepted (proposed by Priya Naidoo, seconded by Sipho Ndlovu).
- The R5 000 deposit for the Silver Oak Function Hall has been paid.
- R18 400 has been raised; the target is R30 000, so R11 600 is still needed.

**TRANSACTIONAL TEXT RUBRIC (25 marks)**

**Content, planning and format (15 marks)**
- **13 to 15, Exceptional:** insightful, original and fully relevant response; purpose, audience and context fully understood; format conventions applied correctly; clearly well planned.
- **10 to 12, Skilful:** relevant, well-developed content; good awareness of purpose and audience; format correct with minor lapses.
- **7 to 9, Moderate:** adequate, relevant content; some awareness of audience; format mostly correct, with some errors or omissions.
- **4 to 6, Elementary:** thin or partly irrelevant content; little awareness of audience; format poorly applied.
- **0 to 3, Inadequate:** irrelevant or confused content; no awareness of format.

**Language, style and editing (10 marks)**
- **9 to 10, Exceptional:** register, tone and style perfectly suited to the purpose and audience; precise vocabulary; virtually error-free.
- **7 to 8, Skilful:** appropriate register; fluent; few errors.
- **5 to 6, Moderate:** register mostly appropriate; adequate language; some errors.
- **3 to 4, Elementary:** register often inappropriate; frequent errors.
- **0 to 2, Inadequate:** so many errors that meaning is largely lost.

**CALCULATING THE MARK**
Content, planning and format ✓ (15) + Language, style and editing ✓ (10) = 25 marks
